name: William Morris
role: English designer, poet and socialist leader (1834-1896)
summary: Morris became a revolutionary socialist in the 1880s and co-founded the Socialist League, which held that all land and means of production must be common property, that wages, exchange and class distinctions would end, and that socialism is international. He distrusted parliament and State Socialism, preferred decentralised, direct popular administration and the general strike, and in News from Nowhere pictured a stateless, pleasure-in-work society with no prisons, armies or nations.

notes: Based on the Gutenberg texts of News from Nowhere, Signs of Change and Hopes and Fears for Art and on Morris's lectures and Commonweal articles at marxists.org (1882-1893). Themes searched: economy and property, state and parliament, law and punishment, marriage and sex, religion, nations, empire, Ireland, war, work and machinery, towns and country, art and ancient buildings, education, trade unions, violence and revolution, anarchism, immigration, animals, technology, ecology. He wrote almost nothing on policing detail, healthcare, immigration policy, drugs, guns, race, gender identity, central banking or tax rates, so those are null. He left the Socialist League in 1890 and later supported the Hammersmith Socialist Society; his core positions were stable across 1884-1893. News from Nowhere is a utopian romance and counts as his stated vision, at medium confidence where nothing else backs it.
